A1.justification: Both PDFs describe the same PluRel research work. Their complete main texts, figures, tables, equations, and Appendices A–D are readable and support reliable comparison.

before.justification: V1 reports original synthetic-data scaling experiments, evaluation on 18 RelBench tasks, computational-efficiency measurements, and QK-normalization ablations.

after.justification: V2 retains the original scaling, RelBench, and ablation results and reports revised computational-efficiency measurements.

M1.justification: Appendix B.2 changes the documented HSBM connectivity rule from congruence modulo the maximum of the two block counts to modulo their minimum. This changes which connections receive probability 0.9 when block counts differ. The three-stage generator and overall RT architecture remain intact; implementation changes are not established.

E1.justification: Both versions use synthetic relational databases and the same six RelBench datasets: rel-amazon, rel-avito, rel-f1, rel-hm, rel-stack, and rel-trial. Coverage remains 10 classification and eight regression tasks, with the same supplementary test scenarios.

E2.justification: Tables 1 and 4 retain Real only, Synthetic only, and Synthetic + Real comparisons. Appendix D.2 retains comparisons with and without QK-Norm. Newly cited database generators are not evaluated as additional baselines.

E3.justification: Table 4 changes the stated pretraining budget of the alternative 512-database checkpoint from 32B to 16B tokens while retaining its numerical entries. This is a reported setting revision, without evidence of rerunning experiments. The main scaling grid, metrics, and leave-one-database-out protocol remain unchanged.

E4.justification: The retained base-model robustness comparison in Table 4 now describes its alternative checkpoint as using 16B rather than 32B tokens. Appendix B.4 also revises the measurements supporting its computational-scaling analysis. No new analysis questions are introduced, and the QK-Norm sensitivity and overfitting analyses remain unchanged.

E5.justification: Both versions report mean and standard deviation across 10 seeds for Table 3, mean and standard error across three seeds for continued pretraining, and four initialization seeds in Appendix D.2. Changed uncertainty values in Table 3 do not change the reporting procedure.

E6.justification: Table 3 substantially revises computational-cost results: latency changes from 147.5 to 2.5 seconds for 10 tables and from 1368.6 to 26.1 seconds for 80 tables. Corresponding peak memory rises from 0.45 to 0.76 GB and from 0.91 to 1.35 GB. The cause is unexplained, so these replacements do not establish a controlled implementation speedup. Predictive numerical entries in Tables 1 and 4 and all plotted results remain unchanged.

T1.justification: Appendix B.2 revises the mathematical definition of HSBM block probabilities from maximum-based to minimum-based modular matching. Appendix D.2 changes the written key-normalization term from RMSNorm(K^T) to RMSNorm(K)^T. Scaling-law formulations and temporal-function definitions are otherwise retained; numbering the existing joint power-law equation adds no theory.

C1.justification: The abstract, introduction, and conclusion retain the same contributions: relational database synthesis, power-law scaling with synthetic diversity and size, transfer to real databases, and benefits from continued real-data pretraining. Their scientific scope is unchanged.

C2.justification: Interpretations concerning underfitting, overfitting, distribution alignment, missing semantics, and schema-sparsity effects remain unchanged. Limitations concerning cyclic/self-referential relationships and supported feature modalities are retained. Revised resource-use statements report changed observations.

D1.justification: V1 explicitly links a GitHub repository for code, models, and data; v2 replaces this with a project-webpage pointer. The appendix revises the documented sampling formula, auxiliary checkpoint budget, and resource estimates, but supplies no explanation of an implementation optimization or hardware change behind the timing revision.

R1.justification: Section 4 adds Houkjær et al. (2006) and Arasu et al. (2011), acknowledging statistical database synthesis for testing analytical applications. This modestly broadens historical positioning. Updating the Relational Transformer citation from its 2025 preprint to its 2026 publication does not introduce a different work.

P1.justification: Changes include publication front matter, a short related-work addition, localized wording edits, and correction of the inconsistent P(i) index to M(i) near Equation 5. The narrative and section/appendix organization are substantially preserved.

P2.justification: Tables 1 and 4 reorder rows by dataset and task while preserving their columns. Publication front matter and text reflow change page placement, including the conclusion continuing onto page 9. All five figures retain identical image content; no figures or tables are added or removed.

improvement.justification: V2 improves precision through the corrected SCM index and clearer QK-normalization formula, while added historical context and ordered result tables modestly improve readability. Core predictive evidence is unchanged. Table 3 reports much lower latency with higher memory use without explaining the revision, so those numbers do not independently establish a quality improvement.
